The Outer Product of the Scores as the Expected Information

Source: R/expect_method.R
expect_opg.Rd

Selects the empirical outer product of the observed scores (OPG, the estimator of Berndt, Hall, Hall and Hausman) as the estimate of an expected derivative. No expectation is taken and nothing is simulated: the quantity that the score identity (see expected_derivative_methods) averages over the model is read at the observations in hand. At order 2 the expected Hessian is replaced, observation by observation, by $$-\,\ell_i(y)\,\ell_j(y),$$ where \(\ell_i\) is the derivative of the log-density with respect to the \(i\)th parameter. At order 3 the expected third derivative is replaced by $$-\left(\ell_{ij}\ell_k + \ell_{ik}\ell_j + \ell_{jk}\ell_i + \ell_i\ell_j\ell_k\right),$$ and at order 4 by the corresponding sum over the partitions of the four indices into at least two blocks, with the sign changed. Every term is a product of observed derivatives of lower order than the target, so the cost is one evaluation of each of those orders and the target order itself is never needed.

The matrix at order 2 is positive semidefinite and has the same fixed point as the expected information, which makes it adequate for the step of Fisher scoring. As an estimate of the information it has the variance of a single product of scores per observation, and at orders 3 and 4 the variance of a product of up to four derivatives; the sum over \(n\) observations converges to \(n\) times the expectation at the rate \(n^{-1/2}\). A standard error should be read from the observed information (see fit_distrib()).

This is the default of distrib_expected_hessian() for a family without a closed form, and of fisher_scoring() and expected_info(). At orders 3 and 4 it is never the default and is never replaced by another method: a call with method = expect_opg() returns the empirical sums of products described above. expected_derivative_methods compares it with the other methods.

Usage

expect_opg()

Value

An S7 object of class ExpectOPG, which inherits from ExpectMethod, with no properties.

See also

expect_integrate() and expect_mc() for the other methods; expected_derivative_methods for the comparison; distrib_expected_hessian(), distrib_deriv3(), distrib_deriv4() and fisher_scoring() for the functions that take the object.

Examples

# A family defined by its density alone has no closed-form information.
Dens <- S7::new_class("DensOPG", parent = continuous_distrib)
S7::method(distrib_pdf, Dens) <- function(distrib, y, theta, log = FALSE, ...) {
  stats::dnorm(y, theta[[1]], theta[[2]], log = log)
}
d <- Dens(distrib_name = "dens", dimension = "univariate",
          bounds = c(-Inf, Inf), params = c("mu", "sigma"),
          params_interpretation = c(mu = "location", sigma = "scale"),
          n_params = 2L,
          params_bounds = list(mu = c(-Inf, Inf), sigma = c(0, Inf)),
          link_params = list(mu = linkfunctions7::identity_link(),
                             sigma = linkfunctions7::log_link()),
          params_smooth = c(mu = TRUE, sigma = TRUE))
th <- list(mu = 0, sigma = 2)
distrib_expected_hessian(d, c(-1, 0.5, 2), th, method = expect_opg())$mu_mu
#> [1] -0.062500 -0.015625 -0.250000

# The same object is accepted at the higher orders.
distrib_deriv3(d, c(-1, 0.5, 2), th, expected = TRUE,
               method = expect_opg())$mu_mu_sigma
#> [1]  0.05468750 -0.07861328  0.50000001

# And it selects the step of Fisher scoring.
fisher_scoring(method = expect_opg())
#> Fisher scoring
#>   expected information: by the outer product of the scores
